prime.problem: One replica holds about 40 req/s of the course workload, so production runs many. An ordinary load balancer spreads requests evenly and splits every prefix cache N ways; a naive cache-affinity router sends every popular prompt to one melting replica; and an autoscaler watching GPU busy % can't tell a full healthy batch from an overloaded one.
prime.fits: First card of group 5, the layer above one engine. It applies the prefix cache (group 3) and admission control (the preemption and concurrency cards) across many replicas: a gateway that sheds load, a router that trades affinity against balance, and an autoscaler on leading signals.
expect: gateway (may it enter?) vs router (where does it go?)
round robin, least-loaded, power of two, sticky, prefix-hash, scored
per-key token buckets and 429 with Retry-After
scale on queue depth and KV use, not GPU busy %
prime.goal: Pick a routing policy for a workload from how its prefixes compare with one replica's cache, compute a scored router's choice, design token-based admission, and choose autoscaling signals that lead rather than lag.

attend: In workload A round robin is fine; in workload B it is 188× worse on TTFT p50. What property of B makes the difference?
Why does prefix consistent hashing leave one replica empty and another with 302 requests in workload A?
With the card's weights, at what load does a warm replica lose its cached request to a cold idle one?
Why should rate limits count tokens rather than requests?
Why is GPU utilisation a misleading autoscaling signal for LLM serving?

must: Each replica has its own prefix cache → pure balance (round robin, least-loaded) spreads every prefix over every replica → when prefixes overflow one cache, LRU evicts what the next request needs (B: 45.6% hits, 2.7 s TTFT p50)
Pure affinity (prefix hashing) keeps hits high → but load follows the hash, not capacity → a few hot prompts pile onto one replica (302 vs 0 requests, 10,459 tok/s)
A scored router adds both terms with weights → it takes the cache hit unless that replica is much busier → best or tied in both workloads (A: 13,076 tok/s; B: 84.5% hits, 73.2 ms p99)

Past capacity a replica's queue makes every request late → the gateway should reject excess early (token buckets, 429 + Retry-After) → autoscale on leading signals (queue depth, KV use) because a new replica takes seconds to load weights
elevated: Normalising load by the busiest replica puts both terms on a 0–1 scale → the weights become an exchange rate ("a hit is worth this much queue") → GKE raised the queue weight from 3 to 5 to steer around hot nodes
reference: vLLM's DP router score (4 × waiting + running)
GKE's 3:3:2 and 3:5:2 weights and the llm-d 57× figure
HPA and KEDA as Kubernetes autoscalers

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the gateway, router, replicas and autoscaler with what each reads and decides. Write the scored-router formula and one line on when round robin is enough and when affinity is everything.
checklist: gateway: auth, token-based rate limits, 429 + Retry-After
prefixes fit every replica's cache → routing barely matters (workload A)
prefixes overflow one cache → affinity is everything (workload B)
autoscale on queue depth and KV use; weights take seconds to load

retrieve.q: Explain why the same round-robin router is fine in workload A and disastrous in workload B.
answer: A: 4 prompts fit easily in every replica's cache, so each replica warms once and hits after that (89.6%)
B: 64 prompts need 8,192 blocks but each replica has 4,000; spreading them everywhere makes each replica evict what the next request needs (45.6%)
the lost hits turn a comfortable load into an overload: TTFT p50 2,690 ms vs 14.3 ms

retrieve.q: Walk through the scored router's decision for a warm replica (hit 0.94) at the maximum load versus a cold idle replica, and again with the warm one at half the maximum load.
answer: busiest warm: 3 × 0.94 − 3 × 1 = −0.18; cold idle: 0 → the cold one wins
warm at half load: 3 × 0.94 − 1.5 = 1.32 → the warm one keeps the request
the weights decide how much queue one cache hit is worth

retrieve.q: Traffic spikes and one replica takes about 8 s to load its weights. Which signals do you scale on, and what absorbs the burst meanwhile?
answer: scale on queue depth and KV use: they rise before TTFT does
at 80 req/s about 642 requests arrive before the new replica serves one
meanwhile the gateway sheds with 429s and headroom on the existing replicas absorbs the rest

compare.q: Cache-aware LPM ordering on one replica and prefix-aware routing across replicas both chase hits. What does each control, and what fairness risk does each carry?
answer: LPM orders the queue inside one replica so warm requests run first
routing decides which replica a request goes to so its prefix is already there
LPM can starve cold-prefix requests; affinity routing can overload the replica with the hot prefix

compare.q: The latency course's model routing picks which model answers; this card's router picks which replica. How do the two layers stack, and what does each optimise?
answer: model routing sits above: it chooses a model tier per request (cost vs quality)
replica routing sits below: it chooses a copy of that model (cache hits vs load)
both can run together: tier first, then the replica holding the prefix

predict.q: Replace prefix-hash with a bounded-load variant: hash as before, but if that replica's load exceeds 1.25 × the mean + 1, try the next replica in the ring. Before running: does it fix workload A's imbalance, and what does it do to workload B's hit rate?
predict.answer: It fixes A's imbalance (requests per replica become 166 / 184 / 109 / 141, throughput 10,459 → 12,266 tok/s, TTFT p99 45.8 → 40.4 ms). In B it costs hits: spilled requests land on replicas without their prefix, so the hit rate falls from 84.5% to 80.6% and TTFT p99 rises from 117.6 to 298.0 ms. Moving load blindly breaks affinity; the scored router moves load only when a replica is much busier, and keeps 84.5% with a 73.2 ms p99 (our run of labs/routing_sim.py with the same seeds).

apply.task: Three small calculations. (a) With 8 system prompts hashed onto 4 replicas, what is the expected number of replicas that get no prompt, and the probability that all 4 get at least one? (b) At 70 req/s, how many requests arrive during one replica's 8.0 s weight load? (c) Using the card's weights, what does a warm replica (hit 0.5) score at maximum load, and does it beat a cold idle replica?
apply.done: (a) 4 × (3/4)⁸ ≈ 0.40 empty replicas expected; P(all 4 used) ≈ 62.3% (by enumeration). (b) 70 × 8.0 = 560 requests. (c) 3 × 0.5 − 3 × 1 = −1.5 < 0, so the cold idle replica (score 0) wins.
apply.hint: For (a), each replica misses a given prompt with probability 3/4, independently for 8 prompts.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether bounded load fixes A, or what it costs in B?
